quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: The morning ferry left the harbor an hour late because a thick fog had settled over the bay.
Passengers who normally read or slept on the crossing stood at the rail, straining to see anything beyond the bow.
The captain slowed the engines and sounded the horn at regular intervals, listening for any reply from other vessels.
Halfway across, a faint horn answered from the left, and the captain steered slightly to the right to keep well clear of it.
A few minutes later, the shape of a large cargo ship slid past, so close that several passengers gasped.
The captain said nothing, but he kept the horn sounding until the shore appeared as a dark line.
When the ferry finally docked, the passengers thanked him warmly, and he replied that the fog had simply asked for patience.
quests.explanation: The fog explains the late departure and the strained watching, the captain's precautions come next, the answering horn is the warning, the passing ship shows how close the danger was, the captain's silence shows his focus, and the docking closes the crossing. "Halfway across" and "a few minutes later" fix the middle of the sequence.
quests.hint: The sentences combine time, cause, and reaction. Which event explains why the passengers gasped, and which earlier action explains why it was safe?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: Several European cities have closed their central districts to private cars, a policy that divides opinion.
Supporters argue that fewer vehicles mean cleaner air, quieter streets, and safer conditions for pedestrians and cyclists.
They point to shopping streets where footfall rose after cars were removed, since people lingered longer and spent more.
Opponents, however, worry about businesses that depend on deliveries and about residents with limited mobility who cannot easily use public transport.
In response, several cities have introduced exemptions and delivery windows so that essential vehicles can still enter at set times.
Studies of these schemes suggest that their success depends less on the ban itself than on the quality of alternatives that accompany it.
Where buses, trains, and cycle routes are reliable, resistance tends to fade, whereas poorly prepared bans provoke lasting hostility.
quests.explanation: The policy is introduced, supporters argue for it, they cite evidence, opponents object, the cities respond with exemptions, studies evaluate the schemes, and the last sentence draws a conclusion from those studies. "These schemes" refers to the bans with their exemptions.
quests.hint: "Opponents, however" and "in response" show a debate developing. Which sentence states the position that the opponents object to, and which sentence records how policy-makers answered them?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: At six in the morning, the hospital's patient records system stopped responding, and staff on the wards could not retrieve medication charts.
The head nurse immediately activated the paper-based emergency procedure, which required nurses to note each dose by hand.
Meanwhile, the IT team traced the fault to a failed server and began restoring the system from the previous night's backup.
The backup was complete, but the process took four hours, during which the wards relied entirely on handwritten notes.
Once the system returned, staff had to enter the handwritten entries into it, checking each one against the original charts.
The hospital's review later concluded that no patient had been harmed, largely because the emergency procedure had been practiced.
It also recommended a second, independent server, since the fault had shown how much depended on a single machine.
quests.explanation: The failure comes first, the nurses' response and the technicians' response run in parallel, the long restoration explains the reliance on paper, the return of the system leads to data entry, the review evaluates what happened, and the recommendation follows from its finding. "It" refers to the review.
quests.hint: Two time words place events in parallel and in sequence. Which sentences do they connect?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: Most people associate the production of oxygen with forests, yet a large share of it comes from microscopic organisms in the sea.
These organisms, called phytoplankton, float near the surface, where they capture sunlight and convert carbon dioxide into sugars.
As they do so, they release oxygen, and it is estimated that they supply roughly half of the oxygen in the atmosphere.
They also form the base of most marine food chains, since small animals feed on them and larger animals feed on those.
Because phytoplankton need both light and nutrients, they flourish where cold, nutrient-rich water rises toward the surface.
Changes in ocean temperature and circulation can therefore alter their distribution and, with it, the fish and birds that depend on them.
Protecting the oceans is consequently a matter of protecting the air as well as the sea.
quests.explanation: The assumption and its correction come first, the organisms are named and described, the oxygen is quantified, a second role is added with "also", their needs explain where they live, "therefore" links changes in the sea to wildlife, and "consequently" links the oceans to the air. Each sentence widens the argument.
quests.hint: "Yet" corrects a common assumption. Which sentence states the assumption, and how do the later sentences build on the correction?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: Among her late father's papers, Renata found an envelope addressed to a man whose name she did not recognize.
The envelope was sealed and unstamped, and the date on the letter inside was more than twenty years old.
The letter apologized for a quarrel over a business, and it ended with an invitation to meet and settle the matter.
Renata hesitated, wondering whether delivering a message so old would be welcome or merely painful.
After a week, she decided that her father would have wanted the apology to reach its reader, and she traced the man through an old directory.
He was elderly now, and when he read the letter, he was silent for a long time before he thanked her.
He explained that he had regretted the quarrel too, and he asked her to tell him about her father's later years.
quests.explanation: The discovery comes first, the letter's condition and date follow, its contents explain its purpose, Renata's doubt is a reaction, her decision follows a week later, the man's response shows the effect, and his explanation reveals that he shared the regret. "Now" contrasts the old man with the past quarrel.
quests.hint: "So old" and "its reader" both point to things described earlier. Which sentences describe them?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: Six months before the annual conference, the organizing committee asked each member to list what had gone wrong the previous year.
The list was long, but three problems appeared repeatedly: unclear signage, late speakers, and too few chairs in the main hall.
The committee agreed to address the problems in order of cost, beginning with signage, which required only a change of design.
For late speakers, they decided to give every presenter a printed schedule with a personal arrival time, ten minutes before the official start.
The shortage of chairs was harder to solve because the hall had a fixed capacity, so the committee limited registration and offered a video link to a second room.
When the conference took place, attendance was slightly lower than before, but participants rated the organization far higher.
The committee concluded that a smaller, well-run event had served the purpose better than a crowded one.
quests.explanation: The review of the previous year comes first, the repeated problems are named, the committee sets an order, the cheap fix comes first, the harder problem comes last, the event tests the solutions, and the conclusion evaluates them. "But" contrasts lower attendance with higher ratings.
quests.hint: Two phrases organize the middle of the paragraph: one names a set of problems and the other sets an order for tackling them. Which sentence introduces the set, and which sets the order?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: A globe is the only accurate model of the Earth, but it is impractical for sailors who need to plot a course across the sea.
In 1569, the cartographer Gerardus Mercator published a flat map with a special arrangement of latitude and longitude lines.
On his map, lines of constant compass direction appeared as straight lines, which allowed navigators to steer by a single bearing.
The price of this convenience was distortion, since areas far from the equator appeared much larger than they really are.
Greenland, for example, looks as large as Africa on such a map, although Africa is about fourteen times bigger.
For centuries, the projection remained standard, and its distortions shaped how many people imagined the relative size of countries.
Modern mapmakers now offer alternatives that preserve area more faithfully, though none of them is ideal for navigation.
quests.explanation: The problem comes first, the invention offers a solution, the advantage is explained, "the price" introduces the drawback, the Greenland example illustrates it, the long-term effect follows, and modern alternatives complete the story. "Such a map" refers to the Mercator map.
quests.hint: A phrase about a price points to an advantage described earlier. Which sentence describes the advantage, and which gives an example of the cost?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: When her father retired, Elsbeth inherited the small hardware shop that her family had run for three generations.
She had a secure job in another city, and running the shop would mean giving it up.
A developer offered to buy the building at a generous price, and her brother urged her to accept.
Elsbeth spent a month working in the shop on weekends, observing customers and studying the accounts.
She found that the shop earned little, but that many regular customers, especially elderly ones, depended on it for advice and small repairs.
She decided to sell the building to the developer on condition that the shop could remain as a tenant on a low rent for ten years.
The developer agreed, and Elsbeth's brother took over the daily work, while she kept her job and helped with the accounts.
quests.explanation: The inheritance creates the dilemma, her job and the developer's offer are the competing options, her month in the shop provides evidence, the evidence shows both weakness and value, the decision combines the options, and the agreement shows how it works. "The shop could remain" answers the customers' dependence.
quests.hint: "On condition that" describes part of a compromise. Which sentences describe the two positions that it combines?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: A touchscreen detects a finger without any buttons, moving parts, or visible sensors.
Most phones use a layer of transparent material that holds a faint electrical charge spread across the glass.
The human body conducts electricity, so when a finger touches the screen, a tiny amount of charge flows toward it.
Sensors at the corners of the screen measure this change, and the device compares the readings to locate the touch.
Because the system depends on conduction, an ordinary glove blocks the signal, whereas a glove with conductive thread does not.
Modern screens can track many touches at once, which makes gestures such as pinching and spreading possible.
Software then interprets these movements as commands, so the same finger can scroll a page, zoom a photograph, or type a message.
quests.explanation: The puzzle comes first, the charged layer is the basis, the finger's conductivity causes the change, the sensors locate it, the gloves show a limit that follows from conduction, multitouch is a further capability, and software gives the movements meaning. "These movements" refers to the gestures.
quests.hint: One phrase refers to a measurable change and another to a dependence on conduction. Which sentences supply them?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: A large chestnut tree stood at the boundary between two gardens, and its branches reached far into both.
In autumn, its leaves and nuts covered the neighbor's lawn, and he complained to its owner several times.
The owner, who loved the tree, insisted that a few weeks of raking were a small price for its shade.
The tension grew until the neighbor threatened to cut the branches himself.
An acquaintance suggested asking a tree surgeon to assess the problem, and both men agreed to share the cost.
The surgeon recommended trimming only the lower branches over the lawn, which would reduce the fall of leaves without harming the tree.
Both men accepted the compromise, and the neighbor, somewhat to his own surprise, began to enjoy the shade in summer.
quests.explanation: The tree and its effects come first, the complaint and the owner's answer set out the two positions, the tension escalates, an outsider suggests an expert, the expert proposes a middle path, and the final sentence shows both men accepting it. "Both men" refers to the neighbor and the owner.
quests.hint: "The compromise" names a solution that appears only after two positions are described. Which sentences describe them?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: Prices of assets, such as houses or shares, sometimes rise far above what their underlying value would justify.
The rise often begins with genuine good news, which attracts the first wave of buyers.
As prices climb, newcomers join in, not because they believe the asset is worth the price but because they expect to sell it for more.
This expectation feeds itself, and each rise convinces more people that the trend will continue indefinitely.
Eventually, the supply of new buyers runs out, and prices stop rising.
Once holders fear a fall, many try to sell at the same time, and prices collapse faster than they had risen.
The lesson that economists draw is that a price rising quickly is not, by itself, evidence that an asset is valuable.
quests.explanation: The general phenomenon comes first, real news begins it, expectation draws in more buyers, the expectation becomes self-reinforcing, buyers eventually run out, fear triggers a collapse, and the lesson is drawn last. "Faster than they had risen" compares the fall with the earlier climb.
quests.hint: "This expectation" refers to something described in an earlier sentence. Which one?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: When Femi became the manager of a small support team, he was eager to show that he could improve its performance.
In his first week, he announced several changes to the schedule and the reporting system.
The team, which had not been consulted, responded with polite silence, and productivity dipped.
A senior colleague told him, privately, that people were following the new rules without believing in them.
Femi withdrew most of his changes and instead spent two weeks asking each member what slowed them down.
Their answers revealed problems that he had never noticed, including a software tool that froze several times a day.
Fixing that tool did more for morale than any of his announcements, and he later described the episode as his real training.
quests.explanation: The ambition comes first, the announced changes follow, the team's reaction is a lack of trust, the colleague explains why, Femi changes his approach, the answers reveal the real issues, and the final sentence evaluates the episode. "Any of his announcements" refers to the changes in the second sentence.
quests.hint: "Instead" and "their answers" both point to earlier events. Which sentences do they refer to?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: Hearing begins when sound waves travel down the ear canal and strike the eardrum, a thin membrane that vibrates in response.
Behind the eardrum, three tiny bones pass the vibrations onward and increase their force.
The last bone presses against a fluid-filled spiral chamber called the cochlea, causing the fluid to ripple.
Inside the cochlea, thousands of tiny hair cells bend as the ripples pass, and each cell responds to a particular pitch.
When a hair cell bends, it generates an electrical signal that travels along the auditory nerve to the brain.
The brain interprets the pattern of signals as words, music, or the noise of a passing vehicle.
Damage to the hair cells cannot currently be repaired, which is why prolonged exposure to loud noise can cause permanent hearing loss.
quests.explanation: The route runs from the ear canal through the eardrum, the bones, the fluid, the hair cells, and the nerve to the brain. "The last bone" only exists after the bones are mentioned, "the ripples" only after the fluid, and "the hair cells" only after the cochlea.
quests.hint: "The ripples" and "the last bone" both point to earlier parts of a physical route. Which parts?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: Before a local referendum on a new stadium, both sides held public meetings and distributed leaflets.
Supporters emphasized jobs and the prestige that a new stadium would bring to the city.
Opponents replied that the money would be better spent on schools and public transport.
An independent group of economists published a report estimating that the stadium would create fewer jobs than supporters claimed but more than opponents admitted.
Both camps welcomed the report selectively, quoting the parts that favored their view.
On voting day, turnout was high, and the proposal was rejected by a narrow margin.
Analysts noted that the debate had been unusually well informed, even though it had not produced agreement.
quests.explanation: The campaign is introduced with both sides, each side's argument follows in turn, an independent report evaluates both, each side uses it selectively, the vote is the outcome, and the analysts reflect on the quality of the debate. "Even though" contrasts good information with continued disagreement.
quests.hint: "Opponents replied" and "both camps" depend on two sides having been introduced. Which sentence introduces both?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: When Jonas opened the door one evening, his old dog, missing for five days, was sitting on the step.
The animal was thin and muddy, and one of its paws was cut.
Jonas carried it inside, washed the wound, and gave it water, which it drank as though it had not seen any for days.
During the following hours, the dog ate a little, slept, and woke occasionally to check that he was still in the room.
In the morning, the veterinarian confirmed that the cut was shallow and that the dog would recover quickly.
Jonas learned later that a farmer twenty kilometers away had seen the dog on a road, and that a lorry driver had taken it partway.
He never discovered how the animal found the rest of the way home, and he preferred not to guess.
quests.explanation: The return comes first, the dog's condition is described, Jonas cares for it, the dog rests, the veterinarian confirms recovery, later information partly explains the journey, and the last sentence admits what remains unknown. "Partway" and "the rest of the way" belong together.
quests.hint: A definite noun and a phrase about the remaining journey refer to details introduced earlier. Which sentences supply them?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: A city council wanted to know whether brighter street lighting would reduce night-time crime in a troubled district.
It replaced the lamps in six streets with brighter ones and left six similar streets unchanged.
For a year, police recorded the number of incidents reported in both groups of streets.
On the newly lit streets, incidents fell by about a fifth, whereas the unchanged streets showed almost no difference.
Adjacent streets, however, recorded a slight rise, which suggested that some offenders had simply moved elsewhere.
The council decided to extend the lighting to the whole district and to watch the neighboring areas carefully.
It also published the data, arguing that other cities could test the idea before spending large sums.
quests.explanation: The question comes first, the design uses lit and unlit streets, the year of recording gathers data, the main result compares the two groups, the side effect qualifies it, the decision responds to both findings, and the publication shares the method. "Simply moved elsewhere" explains the rise.
quests.hint: Two contrast words mark differences in the results. Which sentences do they contrast?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: When the potato first reached Europe from South America in the sixteenth century, many people regarded it with suspicion.
It was unfamiliar, it grew underground, and its leaves resembled those of poisonous plants.
Gradually, farmers discovered that potatoes produced more food per hectare than grain and that they grew well in poor soil.
Governments in some countries encouraged cultivation, and some rulers publicly promoted the new food to reassure their subjects.
By the eighteenth century, the crop had become a staple food for poorer families, particularly in Ireland.
The dependence proved dangerous, since a single disease that destroyed the potato crop in the 1840s caused a devastating famine.
The episode is remembered as a warning about the risks of relying too heavily on one crop.
quests.explanation: Suspicion comes first, its causes follow, farmers discover the advantages, governments encourage growing, the crop becomes a staple, the dependence leads to disaster, and "the episode" names the famine as a lesson. Time phrases from the sixteenth century to the 1840s reinforce the order.
quests.hint: "The dependence" and "the episode" each name something described earlier. Which sentences do they refer to?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: Lila decided to test whether music affected how quickly plants grew, and she chose three identical pots of beans for her science fair project.
She played classical music to one pot for an hour each day, played rock music to another, and left the third in silence.
After four weeks, the plants in all three pots had grown to almost the same height.
Lila felt disappointed, but her teacher pointed out that a result showing no difference was still a result.
Together, they discussed why the experiment might not have shown an effect and what she could have controlled more carefully.
At the fair, Lila presented her findings honestly and explained how she would improve the design.
The judges awarded her a prize for scientific thinking, noting that she had reported what she found instead of what she had hoped for.
quests.explanation: The question and the pots come first, the treatments follow, the outcome is that nothing differed, the student's disappointment is answered by the teacher, they analyze the design, the fair provides an audience, and the judges evaluate her attitude. "What she had hoped for" contrasts with "what she found".
quests.hint: A remark about a result with no difference makes sense only if the experiment has been described. Which sentences describe it?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: For decades, fishing fleets in a northern sea took as many cod as they could catch, and catches were large.
By the 1990s, however, the catches began to shrink, and the fish that were caught grew smaller.
Scientists warned that the stock was being fished faster than it could reproduce.
Governments responded by setting annual quotas, limiting the amount of cod each fleet was allowed to land.
The measures were unpopular at first, since fishermen saw their income fall and doubted the scientists' estimates.
After several years, however, the stock began to recover, and the quotas could be raised gradually.
Fishermen who had opposed the limits came to accept them, acknowledging that a healthy stock was the basis of their livelihood.
quests.explanation: The long period of large catches comes first, the first "however" introduces decline, the scientists give the explanation, governments respond with quotas, the measures are unpopular at first, the second "however" introduces recovery, and the opponents change their minds. "The limits" refers to the quotas.
quests.hint: "However" appears twice, and each time it introduces a change of direction. Which change does each one introduce?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: In November 1895, the German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen was experimenting with electrical discharges in a glass tube.
He noticed that a screen coated with special chemicals glowed faintly across the room, even though the tube was covered.
Convinced that some invisible radiation was passing through the covering, he spent weeks investigating its properties.
He found that it could pass through paper, wood, and flesh, but that denser materials such as bone and metal blocked it.
When he placed his wife's hand between the tube and a photographic plate, the image showed the bones and her ring.
Röntgen called the new radiation X-rays, using the letter for an unknown quantity.
Within months, doctors were using the technique to locate fractures and bullets, and it became one of the most rapidly adopted discoveries in medicine.
quests.explanation: The experiment is set up, an unexpected glow is observed, Röntgen infers an invisible radiation, he investigates what it can pass through, the hand image demonstrates it, he names it, and doctors adopt it. "Even though the tube was covered" explains why the glow was surprising.
quests.hint: "The covering" and "the new radiation" both depend on earlier events. Which sentences introduce them?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: Delivering bad news in writing requires more care than most people expect, because the reader cannot see the writer's expression.
A message that opens with the bad news alone can seem blunt, while one that hides it can seem evasive.
A useful approach is to begin with a brief context that shows the reader why the message is being sent.
The bad news should follow directly, in plain language, without excessive apology or vague phrases.
Immediately afterwards, the writer can explain the reasons, since an explanation received alongside the news is more likely to be accepted.
Where possible, the message should close by describing what happens next, so that the reader is left with a path forward.
Rereading the message aloud before sending it helps to detect a tone that may sound harsher on the page than it was intended.
quests.explanation: The difficulty comes first, two bad options are contrasted, the recommended approach starts with context, the news follows directly, the reasons come immediately afterwards, the close describes what happens next, and the final check comes before sending. Each stage builds on the one before it.
quests.hint: "A useful approach" answers a problem. Which sentences describe the problem, and in what order does the approach place its parts?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: In the early nineteenth century, factory workers in many countries labored twelve hours a day or more, six days a week.
Reformers argued that such hours damaged health, prevented education, and left little time for family life.
Employers replied that shorter hours would raise costs and reduce competitiveness.
Trade unions organized strikes and demonstrations, and in some places, they won shorter days after long campaigns.
In 1914, an American car manufacturer announced an eight-hour day at higher wages, a decision that attracted wide attention.
To many observers' surprise, productivity rose, since rested workers made fewer mistakes and turnover fell.
Over the following decades, the eight-hour day became a legal standard in many countries, though the debate over working time continues.
quests.explanation: The long hours are the problem, reformers criticize them, employers reply, unions campaign, a manufacturer tests the idea, productivity rises and contradicts the employers' prediction, and the standard spreads. "Though" admits that the debate has not ended.
quests.hint: A reaction of surprise refers to a prediction made earlier. Which sentence states that prediction?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: A food allergy occurs when the immune system mistakes a harmless protein in food for a dangerous invader.
On first exposure, the body may produce antibodies without any visible reaction.
On later exposure, these antibodies trigger the release of chemicals such as histamine, which cause symptoms.
The symptoms range from an itchy mouth or a rash to swelling of the throat and difficulty breathing.
Because a severe reaction can develop within minutes, people with serious allergies carry medication that can be injected immediately.
Recent studies suggest that introducing small amounts of certain foods to infants early may reduce the risk of developing allergies.
Parents should nevertheless seek medical advice before trying this, since the safest approach depends on the child's history.
quests.explanation: The definition comes first, the first exposure produces antibodies, the later exposure triggers symptoms, the symptoms are described, the emergency medication responds to the danger, the studies point to prevention, and the final sentence adds a caution. "This" in the last sentence refers to early introduction.
quests.hint: "On later exposure" and "these antibodies" depend on an earlier stage. Which sentence describes it?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: Two weeks before her sister's birthday, Camila still had no idea what to give her.
She remembered that her sister had mentioned admiring a small painting in a friend's home, but she could not recall the painter's name.
A message to the friend produced the name, and a search revealed that the artist lived in the same city.
Camila visited the artist's studio and found that the painting her sister had admired had been sold years earlier.
The artist, touched by the story, offered to paint a smaller version of the same scene in the same colors.
The finished picture arrived the day before the birthday, wrapped in plain paper.
When her sister opened it, she was speechless, and she asked how Camila had remembered something she had said only once.
quests.explanation: The problem comes first, a memory offers a clue, the friend supplies the artist's name, the studio visit reveals the obstacle, the artist proposes a solution, the gift arrives, and the sister's reaction closes the story. "Something she had said only once" refers back to the earlier mention of the painting.
quests.hint: A painting is described as something Camila remembered. Which sentence introduces the memory, and which shows the obstacle that it leads to?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: The human heart beats about a hundred thousand times a day, yet most people never notice it.
Each beat begins in a small group of cells in the upper right chamber, which acts as a natural pacemaker.
These cells generate an electrical signal that spreads across the upper chambers and makes them contract.
The signal then pauses briefly at a junction between the upper and lower chambers, giving the lower chambers time to fill with blood.
After the pause, the signal spreads rapidly through the lower chambers, which contract and push blood to the lungs and the rest of the body.
Afterwards, the heart muscle relaxes, and the cycle begins again with the next signal.
Because the pacemaker cells respond to the body's needs, the heart beats faster during exercise and slower during sleep.
quests.explanation: The overall fact comes first, the pacemaker starts each beat, its signal reaches the upper chambers, the pause allows filling, the signal then reaches the lower chambers, the muscle relaxes and the cycle repeats, and the last sentence explains how the pacemaker adjusts the rate. "Again" marks the repetition.
quests.hint: "The pause" and "the next signal" both refer to points in a repeating cycle. Which sentences do they refer to?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: After a software project finished three months late, the manager arranged a meeting to understand what had happened.
She insisted that the purpose was to learn, not to blame, and she asked each participant to describe what they had seen.
Several developers said that the requirements had changed repeatedly, and that each change had forced them to redo earlier work.
The client's representative replied that the changes had been necessary because the original description had been too vague.
The discussion revealed that neither side had noticed how much each change added to the workload.
The group agreed to introduce a simple form that would show the estimated cost of any change before it was approved.
On the next project, the form reduced the number of changes by a third, and the project finished on schedule.
quests.explanation: The late project is the reason for the meeting, the manager's rule keeps it constructive, the developers state their complaint, the client replies, the discussion reveals a shared blind spot, the group designs a remedy, and the next project tests it. "The form" is introduced before it is used.
quests.hint: A reply answers something that has already been said. Which sentence contains what is being answered?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: Plants cannot move, yet their seeds often travel great distances, and they do so by a variety of methods.
Some seeds, such as those of dandelions, carry tiny parachutes and drift far on the wind.
Others, like coconuts, float on ocean currents for months before they wash ashore and sprout.
A third group relies on animals, producing sweet fruit so that birds or mammals will eat them and drop the seeds elsewhere.
Burrs take a different approach, clinging to fur or clothing until they fall off far from the parent plant.
Each method solves the same problem, which is that seedlings that grow directly beneath a parent plant compete with it for light and water.
Travel therefore increases the chance that at least some seedlings will find room to grow.
quests.explanation: The paradox comes first, the wind method is the first example, the sea method is the second, the animal method is the third, burrs are a variation on the animal approach, "each method" gathers them, and "therefore" states the benefit. "The same problem" refers to competition beneath the parent plant.
quests.hint: "Some", "others" and "a third group" build a list. Which sentence gives the first item, and which explains why the list matters?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: At a weekend flea market, a retired teacher named Gustavo bought a box of old papers for a few coins.
Most of the papers were bills and receipts, but at the bottom, he found a bundle of handwritten pages tied with string.
The pages appeared to be a diary kept during a long sea voyage in the nineteenth century, and the ink had faded in places.
Gustavo photographed each page and showed the images to a historian at the local university.
The historian recognized the name of the ship and confirmed that it had carried emigrants to another continent.
She explained that few personal accounts of that voyage survived, so the diary was of real historical value.
Gustavo donated it to the university's archive, on the condition that a transcription would be published for anyone to read.
quests.explanation: The purchase comes first, the discovery of the pages follows, their nature is described, Gustavo seeks expert help, the historian identifies the ship, she explains the value, and Gustavo donates the diary on condition. "It" in the final sentence refers to the diary.
quests.hint: "The historian" and "the diary" appear as known figures in the later sentences. Which sentences introduce each of them?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: Many parents feel that a bored child needs to be entertained at once, and they hand over a screen or plan an activity.
Some psychologists suggest that this response, though kind, may deprive children of a useful experience.
When nothing is provided, a bored child must generate ideas, and the search for something to do exercises imagination.
Children who invent games, build models, or tell stories in such moments practice skills that structured activities rarely demand.
Constant entertainment, by contrast, can teach a child to wait for stimulation instead of creating it.
This does not mean that parents should abandon their children to idleness or refuse to help when a child is truly distressed.
The argument is simply that a little unstructured time is a resource worth protecting.
quests.explanation: The common practice comes first, psychologists raise a doubt about it, the benefit of unstructured time is explained, examples show the skills gained, the contrast describes the risk of constant entertainment, the qualification prevents a misreading, and the last sentence states the main point. "This does not mean" answers an objection.
quests.hint: "This response" and "by contrast" both refer to something described earlier. Which sentence describes the response, and which describes what it is contrasted with?

quests.title: Cohesion & Transition Markers
quests.coreRule: A coherent paragraph starts with an introductory premise and connects each following sentence using transition markers, chronological words, or pronoun references.
orderedSentences: Tadeusz inherited a bare, overgrown plot behind his house and had only a modest sum to spend on it.
He began by clearing the weeds, which cost nothing but a weekend of hard work.
With the ground exposed, he could see that half of it lay in shade for most of the day, while the other half received full sun.
This observation shaped his plan, since vegetables need sunshine while ferns and hostas thrive in shade.
He therefore spent most of his budget on raised beds for the sunny half and left the shady half for cheap, hardy plants that required little care.
Over the summer, the beds produced more vegetables than his family could eat, and the shady corner filled out without any attention.
Looking back, Tadeusz was glad that he had waited to see the plot before buying anything, since his first idea had been to plant it all with lawn.
quests.explanation: The plot and budget come first, clearing is the free first step, it reveals the sun and shade, that observation shapes the plan, the budget is allocated to fit it, the summer shows the results, and the final reflection returns to the choice of waiting. "His first idea" refers to a plan he abandoned.
quests.hint: A reference and a closing reflection both point to a stage before any spending. Which sentences describe that stage?
